explanations.explanation: Poor is it, friend. Right at the start, the LORD has anointed this speaker to preach good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). Notice who is first in line. No velvet rope at this door.
Rich is a fair guess, friend. But verse 1 sends the good news to the poor. They are first on the speaker’s list (Isaiah 61:1). Nobody has to bring a big bank account to hear it.

Kings would get trumpets and a red carpet, sure. But the text says the good news goes to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). No fanfare mentioned, just good news for people who needed it. That’s a big job for an anointed speaker.
Bind them up. Picture someone wrapping a bandage on a hurting friend. The speaker is sent to bind up the brokenhearted (Isaiah 61:1). Careful hands, friend, that’s the job.

Testing is for cookies in the oven, friend. I poke those with a toothpick all day. The text doesn’t send the speaker to test the brokenhearted. It says bind them up (Isaiah 61:1), and I think binding up is a gentle kind of job.

Sending away would be a door closing. Isaiah 61:1 says something different: the speaker is sent to bind up the brokenhearted. Binding up is no door closing. The brokenhearted are bound up, not sent away.
True. Same verse, next line. The speaker is sent to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners (Isaiah 61:1). Locked doors get a word of freedom.

It’s true, friend. Verse 1 says the speaker is sent to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners (Isaiah 61:1). Prisoners sit right on the list beside the brokenhearted. Easy to skim past when a list runs long.
True, and it’s the same sentence. The year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance sit side by side in Isaiah 61:2. Two things proclaimed together.

Verse 2 puts them in the same breath. First the year of the LORD’s favor, then the day of our God’s vengeance (Isaiah 61:2). So both are proclaimed, and the answer is true. It’s a surprising pair to see next to each other, I’ll give you that.
Comfort, that’s the word. For all who mourn, the speaker is sent to comfort them (Isaiah 61:2). A hand on the shoulder, and no lecture attached.

Correct sounds close, and it even starts with the same letter. But nobody is getting corrected here. Verse 2 says the speaker is sent to comfort all who mourn (Isaiah 61:2). Comfort is the word for the mourners.

Warning would be a siren going off in the bakery. For the mourners, verse 2 says something softer. The speaker is sent to comfort all who mourn (Isaiah 61:2). Someone already hurting gets a soft landing.

Baker, that's the swap: a crown of beauty for ashes (Isaiah 61:3). I've scraped enough burnt cookies off a tray to know ashes are what's left when the batch is done for. Now look at the verb: he is sent "…to give them a crown of beauty for ashes…" Give! Nobody is told to scrub the tray harder first, and I'd be doing a happy hop on my gold base just hearing that.

A ring of gold is a nice thought, friend, but it isn’t in the verse. Verse 3 gives a crown of beauty for ashes. A crown goes on the head and a ring goes on the finger, so it’s a different aisle of the jewelry store.
A royal seal stamps papers, and I respect a good stamp, being a stamper myself. But the text doesn’t give the mourners one. Verse 3 says a crown of beauty for ashes. Ashes out, crown in.
Joy. The mourners get the oil of joy instead of mourning (Isaiah 61:3). Mourning goes out the door and the oil of joy walks in. That’s the whole swap in one line.
Healing is a lovely word, and it fits the heart of this passage. But the exact swap in verse 3 is the oil of joy for mourning. Keep that pair together, friend. Mourning out, joy in.
Peace is a good word too, and plenty of verses use it. But Isaiah 61:3 gives the oil of joy for mourning. The verse doesn’t say oil of peace. Joy is the one that’s poured out here.
Sackcloth never shows up in this passage. For a spirit of despair, the mourners get a garment of praise (Isaiah 61:3). So the answer is false. Despair goes out and praise gets put on.
False, and good eye. The text says a garment of praise for a spirit of despair (Isaiah 61:3). Despair comes off and praise goes on. That’s an outfit with room to dance in.
Oaks of righteousness, friend. Verse 3 says the mourners will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD. Big, rooted and standing tall. Mourners called oaks, that’s quite a name.

Lilies of the field is a famous phrase, since Jesus tells people to consider them (Matthew 6:28). But the name in Isaiah 61:3 is oaks of righteousness. The lilies belong to another passage. Oaks are the tough ones.

Reeds by the water bend easy, so it’s a fair guess for something growing. But verse 3 says they will be called oaks of righteousness. They are the planting of the LORD. Reeds aren’t in this verse, oaks are.
So He may be glorified. Verse 3 ends with exactly that: the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified (Isaiah 61:3). The oaks point back at Him. It’s all for His glory.

explanations.answer: So they may rule the nations
explanations.explanation: Ruling the nations is a big picture, but verse 3 doesn’t say it. It says they are the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified. That’s the reason the text gives. Check the ending of the verse, friend.
Resting forever sounds great after all that mourning. But verse 3 doesn’t give it as the reason. It says the LORD plants them that He may be glorified (Isaiah 61:3). His glory is the stated purpose.
Rebuild them. Verse 4 says they will rebuild the ancient ruins, restore the places long devastated and renew the ruined cities. Three verbs, all aimed at the rubble. Mourners turned builders.
Mourning is where they started, back in verse 3. By verse 4 they have work to do. They will rebuild the ancient ruins (Isaiah 61:4). I think the hammers are coming out.

Leaving the ruins would be the easy road. Verse 4 says the opposite. They will rebuild the ancient ruins, restore the places long devastated and renew the ruined cities. Those desolations of many generations get fixed, not forgotten.

True. Verse 6 begins with “But you will be called the priests of the LORD…” and goes on to say they will be spoken of as ministers of our God. The strangers handle flocks and fields in verse 5. God’s people are the ones called priests.
Verse 6 says it plainly: “But you will be called the priests of the LORD…” They will be spoken of as ministers of our God, so the answer is true. The title is theirs, friend.
True. Verse 6 says you will feed on the wealth of nations. Verse 5 has foreigners working as plowmen and vinedressers. The people also get to boast in the riches of the nations (Isaiah 61:6).

It’s true, friend. Verse 6 says God’s people will feed on the wealth of nations and boast in their riches. Verse 5 just before it has foreigners as plowmen and vinedressers. Both lines are right there in the passage.
Portion. Verse 7 says, “Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion…” Shame leaves and a double share arrives. That’s a better exchange than any I’ve made.
Burden is the opposite flavor, friend. Shame gets replaced, not doubled. Verse 7 says a double portion instead of shame.
Debt sounds like what bills are made of. But verse 7 says instead of shame, a double portion. Debt isn’t anywhere in the passage. Good thing, because nobody wants a doubled-up bill.
Justice. The LORD says, “For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity…” (Isaiah 61:8). He puts both on the table, what He loves and what He hates. Clear as a freshly wiped counter.
Sacrifice is a big word in the Bible, but verse 8 doesn’t use it here. The LORD says He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity (Isaiah 61:8). Justice is the one He names.

Wealth does show up in this passage, in verse 6, where they feed on the wealth of nations. But when the LORD says what He loves in verse 8, the word is justice. Robbery and iniquity are on the hate side (Isaiah 61:8).
Verse 9 says the opposite. Their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples (Isaiah 61:9). So the answer is false. Known, not hidden.
False, you’ve got it. Verse 9 says their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. These folks get noticed.
Blessed. Verse 9 says, “All who see them will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed.” People will see it with their own eyes. All who see them will say so.
Scattered would make this a sad verse, but it isn’t one. Isaiah 61:9 says all who see them will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed. The word is blessed, friend.

Humbled is close to humiliation, which verse 7 sends away. But the last word of verse 9 is blessed. Everyone who sees these descendants will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed (Isaiah 61:9).

explanations.answer: God has clothed me with salvation
explanations.explanation: That’s the reason. Verse 10 says, “…He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness…” The rejoicing comes because of what God has done. It’s about the garments He gave.

explanations.answer: God has given me a long life
explanations.explanation: A long life is a gift, but it isn’t the reason in this verse. The reason given is “for He has clothed me with garments of salvation…” (Isaiah 61:10). The text doesn’t mention years at all. It’s about the clothing.

explanations.answer: God has made me a great king
explanations.explanation: A great king would be a fine thing to announce, but the passage doesn’t say it here. Verse 10 gives the reason: He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness. No crown is mentioned for this speaker. The joy comes from the clothing God gave.

explanations.answer: A bridegroom and a bride dressed up
explanations.explanation: A bridegroom and a bride dressed up. Verse 10 says it is as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels. Two people dressed for a wedding. That’s the picture the passage paints.

explanations.answer: A king dressed for his crowning
explanations.explanation: A crowning would be a grand picture, but it isn’t the one in the verse. Isaiah 61:10 compares it to a bridegroom with a priestly headdress and a bride with her jewels. The comparison is a wedding, not a coronation.

Battle gear would make for a very different outfit. Verse 10 shows a wedding: a bridegroom wearing a priestly headdress and a bride adorning herself with her jewels. No armor anywhere in the verse. Just two people dressed up for a happy day.
Praise. Verse 11 says, “…the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.” Like seeds coming up in a garden. And the nations get a front-row seat.
Peace is a good word, and it’s close in spirit. But the verse says righteousness and praise will spring up (Isaiah 61:11). The garden picture belongs to those two. Seed goes in, praise comes up.

Plenty sounds like a garden word, I’ll give you that. But the verse pairs righteousness with praise, not plenty. The Lord GOD will cause both to spring up before all the nations (Isaiah 61:11). Praise is the one.
